subtopic: SALARY REVISIONS-REQUEST FOR TABLING OF DOCUMENTS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last two days 1 have heard a large number of complaints about the revised salary schedules which were tabled on Wednesday. There is a great deal of puzzlement, to say the least, over the fact that a member's principal secretary's salary has been frozen, while the top executive category, already paid over $40,000 per year, receives a full 6 per cent permanent increase.
While accepting that a readjustment in all salary levels is necessary to correct any overclassification which may have occurred, I think morale has been harmed by the selective and mysterious manner in which this occurred. I, therefore, ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That this House requests the tabling of all documents, papers and memoranda on which House of Commons staff salary revisions, tabled in this House on May 31, were based, particularly those which compare House of Commons classifications with public service classifications and those which explain the differentials between positions within the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: COMMITTEE STUDY OF LAW ON SOLICITING, VAGRANCY AND PROSTITUTION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of serious and pressing necessity. For the law to be respected and obeyed, it must be clear, concise and free from ambiguity. Every Canadian, according to our system of jurisprudence, is entitled to know what the law is.
In light of the former changes in the law contained in the Criminal Code of Canada as to soliciting, vagrancy and prostitution, and in the words of one judge, persons will be tried for offences which are not contrary to the law but merely for publicity purposes, creating a false, unnatural, and unwarranted punishment, and in light of the fact that in some places certain police enforcement officers are used as decoys as a method of cracking down on activities that may or may not be illegal, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That the questions of soliciting, vagrancy and prostitution be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs for study and recommendation, with the right of the committee to hear witnesses giving their views and opinions with reference to all matters pertaining to the same.

subtopic: INSPECTION PROCEDURES TO ENSURE MEAT AND LIVESTOCK FREE OF DES CHEMICAL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
INSPECTION PROCEDURES TO ENSURE MEAT AND LIVESTOCK FREE OF DES CHEMICAL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In 1974, the Canadian government banned the use of diethylstilbestrol or DES, a carcinogenic growth hormone which was fed to cattle to promote weight gain. I have just learned that "Radio Noon", a CBC Toronto program, has tested ten samples of beef liver, five Canadian and five American, from four different stores. Despite the ban, nine of these samples were found to contain DES with a level as high as 3,720 parts per billion. Levels as low as two parts per billion have been shown to be toxic in tests of laboratory animals. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):
That this House call for an immediate investigation of the inspection procedures for meat and livestock products imported into Canada and produced in Canada to determine the reasons for the failure of the DES ban and to make recommendations for any changes necessary to avoid a repetition of this problem.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance, who telephoned me this morning to describe the position he had taken in the unsuccessful negotiations with the province of Quebec yesterday regarding the sales tax question. The minister confirmed in that telephone conversation that the federal government continues to refuse the kind of direct payment to the provinces, particularly to the province of Quebec, that is sought by the National Assembly of Quebec and is accorded to every other province. The House knows that there is no regular tax transfer agreement with Quebec. Why did the Minister of Finance of Canada not accept a one-time only tax transfer agreement covering the $100 abatement?
June 2, 1978

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am responding exactly to the wish of the Leader of the Opposition as expressed in a speech he delivered Sunday last when he said: We demand that the equivalent of the amount represented by the tax cut, that is $226 million, be paid in full to the province of Quebec. And we have decided to transfer back to Quebec residents the equivalent of $226 million as requested by the Leader of the Opposition.
Of course, yesterday we tried to make two proposals to the Quebec government, the first one along the lines of Mr. Ryan's formula whereby the tax income reduction would be made in 1978 instead of 1977 but Mr. Parizeau rejected it. We tried to make a further proposal which would have caused me to accept some of his proposals if he were prepared to accept some of mine and he refused. I stated on many occasions yesterday that obviously Mr. Parizeau and the Quebec government have only one thing in mind, to prove that there is no way to deal with the federal government. What we are trying to do is to develop a national policy on economic incentives, and economic success for the Canadian government is certainly not something which meets the political purposes of the separatist government in the province of Quebec.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
The minister was a little more clearcut in his attribution of this proposal to Mr. Ryan in his statement than he was in his communique. In his press communique, he said it was not the same as, but similar to, the proposal made by Mr. Ryan. I am sure Mr. Ryan will be quite prepared to clarify that difference himself.
1 am pleased to know that the minister is now reading and quoting my excellent speeches: that might redound to the better governing of the country. He knows the difference between what we proposed and what he has done. We have proposed to let the government of Quebec, as with the governments of other provinces, have that money. He is proposing some form of payment via individual citizens. He is proposing to change the system with the province of Quebec.
My question is this: In the second proposal that the Minister of Finance made yesterday, according to his communique he proposed to make a one-time only transfer to the province of Quebec on condition that the Government of Canada is allowed to dictate the way a province uses a provincial jurisdiction. The minister knows that that condition is unacceptable to the government of Quebec. He knows it is unacceptable to Mr. Ryan. Indeed, it is unacceptable to anyone else who respects the constitution of Canada. The minister is prepared to make a one-time only tax transfer in a way that violates the constitution. My question is quite simple: Why will he not agree to make it in a way that respects the constitution of Canada?
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am respecting the constitution all the way. Mr. Parizeau, or any government, can do what they want in their field. In fact, Mr. Parizeau has done it so much that he has selectively cut the sales tax for 12 months. It is done. I have not intervened. As there is no agreement with Mr. Parizeau, and he does not want an agreement, I do not want to penalize the citizens of Quebec. I am reducing the income tax of Quebeckers in exactly the same way as I have done for those in Ontario and New Brunswick. On the night of the budget I reduced the federal income tax by $100. They increased their provincial sales tax by $100 and followed a procedure of cutting the sales tax.
What I did on the night of the budget was reduce the income tax of the other provinces which have sales tax. 1 have no agreement with Quebec. 1 tried to get an agreement. I made five different proposals. There is no way I can get any agreement with them. 1 am doing now exactly what I did on the night of the budget with the other provinces in reducing the income tax.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: The Minister of Finance must, surely, by now recognize that it is not exactly the same when the citizens of one province receive a cheque from the federal government and the citizens of other provinces do not receive a cheque. That is not the same.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
One of the proposals that the federal government has put forward-it is one that we on this side of the House would like to see considered with some calm-has the serious disadvantage of delaying the economic stimulus in Quebec for at least a year. Indeed, it may have the consequence of forcing the Quebec government to raise taxes, which it is not in a position to do with ease before that time. Naturally, the chief victims of an arrangement like that will be the people of the province of Quebec.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance this question: Assuming there is some progress affecting the tax year 1978- affecting that proposal-would the federal government be prepared to give the most serious consideration to including in any agreement that might be arrived at, some provision that might bring stimulus to the province, the economy and the people of Quebec this year, when it is needed, rather than causing the people of that province to suffer because of a determination to disagree on the part of two governments?

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
That is exactly why I decided to take the list of the taxpayers of 1977, to make sure that the money was available to assist the Quebec economy this summer. The one disadvantage of the Ryan formula would be that the money would be in the hands of the taxpayers of Quebec only in the spring of 1979. In order to stimulate the economy right now, 1 have decided to go with the taxpayers' list of 1977. If the hon. gentleman would prefer me to take the 1978 list, 1 could do

June 2, 1978
Oral Questions
that; but the money would be in the pockets of federal taxpayers only in the spring of 1979. That was the formula proposed by Mr. Ryan, and I am willing to go along even if, economically, it makes less sense than what I have proposed.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
We all know what has been proposed by Mr. Ryan. His position is far clearer than that taken by the Government of Canada. Yesterday the minister apparently indicated some willingness to accept the 1978 base, something which would have delayed a certain economic stimulus to the economy of that province this year, when it is needed, as the hon. gentleman has just admitted. I hear that the former minister disagrees with the present minister. I know that the Liberal caucus is full of disagreement on this question. But let members opposite resolve their differences internally, and let the Minister of Finance address himself to the question I have asked.
Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal of talking and shouting going on over there. I know how nervous they are about this subject, but 1 ask the Minister of Finance to address himself to the question I put to him. If he does come back to that proposal to move to the 1978 base, will he undertake to enter into some arrangement with the province of Quebec? 1 do not know what it might be.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: We are quite prepared to propose a number of them. One would simply be to respect the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec and to end this attempt to interfere with provincial jurisdiction.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: But the government refuses to do that.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: They want a confrontation.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: I ask the minister, seriously, in the interests of the taxpayers of Quebec and in the interest of equity, to give us an undertaking in principle that if there is to be an agreement relating to 1978, he will ensure that the people of Quebec will not become victims, economically, of this dispute between two governments which appear to be increasingly stubborn?

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: I say, again, to make sure that the Quebec people will not suffer at all, that if the hon. member will vote on the bill today, the cheques will be in the mail next month.

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: QUEBEC SALES TAX-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
I called the hon. member this morning because I thought he had some problem of understanding. It appears my call was not very useful. I repeat that I am not interfering in the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec. They have cut their sales taxes in the way they wished. They can cut all the taxes in their field they wish. They would go bankrupt very quickly-they are close to it-but there is nothing 1 can do about it. It is within their jurisdiction. I am reducing

personal income tax for the federal taxpayers of the province of Quebec.

The minister has indicated that the Ryan proposal, as one way of extricating us from this mess, is not the best one in terms of stimulating the economy of the province. Upon reflection, I agree with him. In this respect the minister at least agrees with the government of Quebec. That government, too, rejected the Ryan formula as not providing the kind of stimulus needed this year.
If that is so, would the minister confirm that the second part of his so-called new proposal for selective sales tax cuts is, in its substance, precisely the same as his original proposal, in the sense that the federal government is still insisting that the Quebec government cut for some period of time all the sales taxes in that province as a condition of getting any federal payment at all?

No, Mr. Speaker, it is a condition that we have a collection agreement. Since Maurice Duplessis there has been no collection agreement between the federal government and the Quebec provincial government. If the hon. member now recognizes that the Ryan formula is not perfect, why did he move a motion in the House of Commons on Thursday, May 25, urging me to accept the Ryan formula?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated the minister's remarks earlier today regarding his proposals. I would have thought that he would at least do the courtesy of reciprocating an attitude which I have. As I said, on reflection-not just today, but previous to today-I have seen the implications of the Ryan formula. I am appealing to the federal government to show the same flexibility as some of the rest of us in this country are prepared to show in this matter.
As I understand the second part of the minister's proposal, that is, the selective sales tax proposal remaining in the province of Quebec, with some subsidization coming in direct payment from the federal government, it is still an insistence by the federal government that the province of Quebec impose a unive nuales tax on all commodities. If that is the case, would the minister not agree that he has come all the way back to his original proposal, which still amounts to his insisting that the federal government impose certain priorities on the provincial government which are within the constitutional right of that province?

Mr. Speaker, in my second proposition of yesterday I came a long way. I said that even if I did not agree with the selective sales tax system proposed by the Quebec government, I would pay part of it. Quebec could have it forever, if it wanted, but I would pay two-thirds for nine months, as I have agreed to do for Saskatchewan and British Columbia. There was some money left over on the table. I said
June 2, 1978

that if Quebec wanted a tax agreement, with that money it could cut sales taxes across the board for the rest of the items until October.

Mr. Speaker, with all respect, I say that the minister is showing an inflexibility which simply is not required in the circumstances. Would the minister confirm that what the Quebec government wants is no more money than any other province?
Second, would the minister agree, because this has not been challenged in the debate, with the fact that I put on the record more than a week ago, that the job impact of the tax cut proposal coming from the province of Quebec would likely create more jobs in the province of Ontario than in the province of Quebec, and as such it is not a balkanization measure?
If the minister agrees with both those points, why can he not admit frankly that he was mistaken in his original judgment, and accept the proposal of the Quebec government?

Mr. Speaker, there are two reasons. Mr. Parizeau made his cut 48 hours after my budget. Before 1 rejected that, I took the liberty of calling some other ministers of finance in this land to ask them if the Quebec proposal was acceptable to them. They said no. I called three. We had previously had a unanimous agreement, so I did not have to call everybody. After I had called three, I knew there was no possibility of agreement, so I could not accept the proposal at that time.
Who were the three?

In addition, Mr. Parizeau went for a full year. British Columbia cut its sales tax by two points for a full year although I recognized only nine months. Following that, they are on their own. I do not see why Quebec should not be on its own after nine months, like British Columbia.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also to the Minister of Finance. Yesterday, in fact, he reopened the discussions with the province of Quebec about changes in the sales tax issue. I should like to ask if he has undertaken to have similar discussions with the governments of the other provinces, notably the government of Manitoba, which had originally proposed to use 1 per cent of the sales tax reduction for direct job-creation programs, and also with the province of Alberta which had been ignored in any discussion of income tax rebates.
Has the minister, therefore, reopened discussions with the other provinces, now that he has proposed making changes on the whole sales tax issue with one province?
[ Translation]

It is very simple, Mr. Speaker. I discussed it with all finance ministers prior to
Oral Questions
the budget. I asked Alberta: Can I help you reduce your sales tax? The minister said: I do not have any. So that settled the matter. I told him: There will be other measures in the budget to help the economy of Alberta. That was settled. In Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and in all provinces, what I did was reduce the income tax on budget night so that they could increase theirs. What I propose today for Quebec is to reduce the income tax for Quebec residents. The Quebec minister of finance can do what he wants in his jurisdiction. He can cut the taxes he wants, that is his business. As for me, I am cutting the income tax of Quebec taxpayers.

Given the fact that the Minister of Finance went into such detail this morning to explain that he had made different arrangements, or had proposed different arrangements, I would have thought he would have considered it courteous, at least, to have conveyed that information to his counterparts in the other provinces.
I should like to ask a supplementary question. Because of the uncertainty and confusion which now surrounds this entire sales tax issue, because of the fact that there would be real interest in the other provinces if any changes were contemplated to be put into effect, and because by its actions of yesterday the Government of Canada has indicated that it really has no clear idea as to where this issue will eventually take us, will the minister, in the interests of common sense and, more important, in the interests of national unity, agree to withdraw the bill from debate in the House at the present time until negotiations with the province of Quebec and, indeed, with the other provinces have been completed?

Mr. Speaker, we are reducing the federal income tax for the federal taxpayers in Quebec. I am acting within my jurisdiction, and Mr. Parizeau can do whatever he wants in his own jurisdiction. But I want to tell the hon. member something, that it will not be the separatist government of Quebec which will run the economic affairs of this nation.

subsubtopic: CUBAN INVOLVEMENT IN AFRICAN HOSTILITIES-CESSATION OF AID TO CUBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yesterday the minister denied that anyone had claimed that Cubans were involved in the Zaire situation. Today, the Carter administration, which is providing evidence that Cuban soldiers in Angola played a role in the Katangan invasion of Shaba province in Zaire, is preparing special broadcasts to tell the Cuban people how Cuban troops are being used as a surrogate force to advance Soviet strategic aims in Africa, and is further backing up its claim by consider-

June 2, 1978
Oral Questions
ing the cancellation of U.S. charter flights to Cuba and the cancellation of athletic exchange programs.
Since there is a split between the American and Canadian view of Cuban involvement in Zaire, will the Canadian government now revise its view and take similar steps to those taken by the Carter administration to pressure Cuba to get out of Africa.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CUBAN INVOLVEMENT IN AFRICAN HOSTILITIES-CESSATION OF AID TO CUBA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all, I have not seen the report to which the hon. member refers; however, I am sure it is an accurate assessment. I do not think it reflects any split. I said yesterday that there was no hard evidence; certainly, the impression I wanted to convey was that there was no hard evidence-

subsubtopic: CUBAN INVOLVEMENT IN AFRICAN HOSTILITIES-CESSATION OF AID TO CUBA
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CUBAN INVOLVEMENT IN AFRICAN HOSTILITIES-CESSATION OF AID TO CUBA
speechtext:
I cannot answer and listen at the same time. Maybe the hon. member would give me the opportunity to answer him; then I will be glad to deal with a supplementary question.
I do not think there is any question that there are Cubans in Angola. Therefore, it is a reasonable assumption that there is some relationship between that and the activities in Zaire. I was simply stating the fact that it was not a proven situation and that a number of countries-among them, Great Britain, The Netherlands, Denmark and Belgium, to name just a few-at least five or six, made the point that it had not been specifically proven in the case of Zaire. That is not to say-I repeat-that anyone is condoning Cuban, Soviet or other interventions in Africa.
In terms of what the United States is now doing, I have had consultations with Secretary of State Vance. I repeat to the House what I said yesterday, that if there is any way, either through the Security Council or through other initiatives taken by the United States or other allies, whether they be in NATO or elsewhere, to end foreign interventions in Africa, we will be fully supportive of them and we will use whatever techniques appear to be most appropriate in our circumstances to reinforce that view.

subsubtopic: CUBAN INVOLVEMENT IN AFRICAN HOSTILITIES-CESSATION OF AID TO CUBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the first point, Zbigniew Brzezinski, special adviser to the president, said:
Any sensible person who sees what is going on in Angola will reach a very obvious conclusion.
This relates to the Cuban involvement in Zaire. I want to ask the minister a supplementary question. Since Canada has provided $13.3 million in aid to Cuba in the last three years, will the minister now formally terminate that aid, as distinct from just letting it run down, to enable Canada to go before the UN Security Council with some credibility in urging that body to give immediate study to the grave implications of Cuba having a total of 43,000 troops in 14 African nations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CUBAN INVOLVEMENT IN AFRICAN HOSTILITIES-CESSATION OF AID TO CUBA

Mr. Speaker, in the first instance, the hon. member uses a highly selective technique. He quotes Mr. Brzezinski without acknowledging that, of course, there is
[Mr. Roche.1
quite a substantial difference of opinion even within the U.S. administration. There have been a number of spokesmen, including the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, who have expressed a quite different view. However, that is beside the point in this regard.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 direct my question to the Minister of Fisheries. In view of the report tabled in the House, in response to question No. 135, which stated that an assistant deputy minister of fisheries, now retired on full pension and appointed as chairman of the Canadian Saltfish Corporation, has been given $62,750 worth of consulting contracts by the government within the past two years as a means of providing some money to him, I ask the minister whether he would seriously consider designating the chairmanship of the corporation as a salaried position so that the fishermen can see directly whether they are getting value for their money.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBIanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FISHERIES-STATUS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FISHERIES RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the past few weeks the government has encountered several difficulties with respect to the implementation of the 1978 Canada-U.S.A. interim fisheries agreement on both the Pacific and Atlantic coasts.
On the Pacific coast the problem relates to the terms under which Canadian fishermen would be allowed access to waters in Washington state to troll for salmon.
June 2, 1978

On the Atlantic coast the problem relates to unrestricted U.S. scallop and pollock fisheries in the Gulf of Maine-Georges Bank area, and what we view as excessive allowable U.S. catch levels for cod and haddock.
These difficulties were discussed at a meeting between Canada and U.S. officials in Washington on April 28, and at meetings between the Canadian and U.S.A. special negotiators for maritime boundaries in Ottawa on May 11 and 12, and again in Washington on May 26. At the May 26 meeting and during subsequent conversations, it has become clear that these problems cannot be resolved in a way that would protect Canadian interests.
My colleagues and I have come to the reluctant conclusion that the 1978 interim reciprocal fishery agreement cannot be implemented by the U.S. in a manner compatible with preserving and protecting our fisheries interests. Accordingly, I wish to announce that the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs has called in the United States ambassador and given him a diplomatic note stating that the Government of Canada is not prepared at this time to continue provisional implementation of the agreement. The note states that, consequently, U.S. fishing vessels will not be permitted to continue fishing operations in Canadian fisheries waters after 12 noon June 4. This means, of course, that the U.S. will take corresponding action against Canadian fishing vessels in U.S. waters.
The government has taken this action with great reluctance, but under the circumstances we believe it is the most appropriate means of maintaining a balance between the fishing interests of the two countries. I am confident that we can work out, on a co-operative basis, enforcement arrangements in the boundary regions that will avoid confrontation.
The problems we have experienced with the interim agreement demonstrate clearly the need for an early settlement of maritime boundaries and for a long term agreement on reciprocal fishing. My colleagues and I continue to believe that a comprehensive maritime boundaries-resources agreement, arrived at by negotiations, is the preferred means of providing for the effective and mutually beneficial management of maritime resources in Canada-U.S.A. boundary areas.
The government recognized that, in negotiating an over-all agreement of this kind, difficult problems remain for both sides in reconciling the various regional and industry interests. At the same time, it has become clear that a balanced and equitable agreement cannot be constructed on the basis of continued insistence by all concerned on their maximum demands. The difficulties which have led to the government's present decision are the best evidence of the need to replace a generalized interim agreement without institutional arrangements by a permanent, comprehensive agreement that places all the issues in an interrelated framework and includes effective mechanisms for interpreting the agreement and for the settlement of differences.
Fisheries
Ambassador Cadieux has been instructed to resume his negotiations and has been in touch with the U.S. negotiator, Ambassador Cutler, and they both agree that the suspension of the interim agreement need not and should not impede their negotiations which, as you know from the joint reports issued in October and March, have laid the basis for progress toward a comprehensive agreement. Thus, in an exchange of letters which is being released, the two negotiators have agreed to resume their negotiations on the long-term agreement. They have scheduled for June 19 and 20 the first of a series of meetings that are intended to lead to early recommendations on a comprehensive agreement.

subsubtopic: FISHERIES-STATUS OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FISHERIES RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the statement by the Secretary of State for Exernal Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) on the present status of the Canada-United States fisheries relations. While agreeing with the action that has been taken, it is a matter of some regret that it has become impossible to implement the 1978 Canada-U.S.A. interim fisheries agreement on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts.
It is my understanding that the 1978 interim agreement, intended to redress the 1977 situation on the west coast by providing for Canadian salmon fishing three to 12 miles, for an additional 54 miles along the United States coast. The United States wanted Canada to agree, categorically, not to fish salmon returning to U.S. waters, namely, Swiftsure Bank, as a conservation measure. We agree to this proposal as long as there was a conservation problem, and the area was closed for at least the last two or three years. But there is no conservation problem today in this area, so Canada did not agree to close down salmon fishing operations and the United States withdrew concessions for the additional 54 miles.
In the meantime, while agreement was provisionally applied, United States fishermen went to court under the acts in the United States to force enforcement. I believe this injunction will apply to Washington, Oregon, and California, but I do not believe it will apply to Alaska halibut-the minister can correct me if I am wrong-nor will it apply on the Atlantic coast. With this precedent on the west coast, however, the door to further difficulties is wide open. For example, on the Atlantic coast the 1978 interim fisheries agreement calls for the 1976 allocations as made by ICNAF for Georges Bank. The total allowable catch for 1976 amounted to 20,000 metric tons of cod and 6,000 metric tons of haddock, of which Canada received 15,600 tons of cod and 4,730 tons of haddock, with the balance allocated to the United States.
In 1977, however, the United States set domestic total allowable catches for cod and haddock at 20,000 metric tons for codfish and 6,000 metric tons for haddock, in other words, a 40 per cent increase in their fishing effort. That is an effort which took the whole total quota allocation as set by the scientists and by the officials of ICNAF for this area.
To add to the problem, in November the United States unilaterally further raised its allocations of cod and haddock to
6004

June 2, 1978
Fisheries
21,600 metric tons of cod and 10,500 metric tons of haddock simply by changing what is called their "by-catch" regulations, thus contravening section 8 of the 1977 agreement.
We must ask why the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) was silent when he knew this was happening. Why was the Secretary of State for External Affairs silent? Why did this matter not come up for discussion with U.S. officials over a year ago?
In the same area, in 1977, there was no management plan established by the United States for pollock or scallops. The U.S. overfished its pollock allocation by something like 3,000 metric tons on Georges Bank alone, and its allocation at that time was something like 6,000 metric tons. Why did the minister not raise his voice when he became aware of these facts?
We imposed quotas and restrictions on our scallop fishermen, for example, Mr. Speaker. We dragged them from Nova Scotia to a meeting here in Ottawa, and then in turn we had to drag the minister to Halifax in order to get a dispute settled that simply asked for the right of Nova Scotian fishermen to catch 850,000 pounds of scallops when the inshore ground fishery declined. This right was denied them by the minister, and he argued and fought over the matter for a period of some two months. While we did this to our own fishermen, the United States increased its scallop effort by 120 per cent in one year, and they increased their catch in one year by 180 per cent. Did this government complain? Well, if they did, where are the complaints on the record?
Overfishing of pollock and of scallops cannot help but result in lower total allowable catches for both species in future years. The United States will now most likely argue for a greater share in the future of all species based on their recent high percentages.
The situation to date in 1978 is obviously the same, with no plans, as far as I know, for total allowable catches of pollock or scallops by the United States, and with the United States claiming the "total" allocated for this area.
The 1977 fishing facts were known a long time ago. Steps should then have been taken to consult with the United States so that no further action would be taken without consultation. Unfortunately, public action has already prejudiced the situation. For example, how can the government expect Canadian fishermen to remain within their pollock quotas, in a fishery which comes under joint management between Canada and the United States, in the face of open quotas and in the face of open fishing effort by the United States fleet?
The action taken by the United States in ignoring the International Commission for North Atlantic Fisheries quotas is highly irrational in the face of joint scientific recommendations for this area. We obviously need a joint fisheries management plan for scallops. Canadian fishermen are now paying a very heavy price for the procrastinating policies of this government. Only yesterday, when asked whether this matter was discussed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he was
[Mr. Crouse.l
in the United States, his response was-and I am paraphrasing-that there were too many other important things. There was no time for this fisheries problem. It seems there is only time for fisheries problems of this nature when there is an election on the agenda. But, in between, Mr. Speaker, there is no time for the fishermen and their problems.
In conclusion, I say to you that it is not helpful when the headlines scream "Canada Declares 'War' on U.S. fishermen". It is not helpful in any way whatsoever, because the U.S. buys some 70 per cent of our catch and is our most important customer. I hope that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have learned a lesson from what has happened and that they will be more diligent in their activities in trying to secure a resolution to what could be a very serious economic problem, not only in Nova Scotia but throughout the entire length and breadth of Atlantic Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the regrettable news that we have today, and I will elaborate on it in a moment, could not be a better symbol of the way in which the Government of Canada deals on the one hand with Canadian economic or job interest and, on the other hand, deals internally with our provincial governments.
Earlier today we saw the tough talking federal government in its response to a federal-provincial relationship issue. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is always ready to sort of loosen his tie, take off his jacket, and talk tough when it comes to dealing with other provinces in Canada, a sublimely inappropriate attitude in terms of federal-provincial relationships. But when it comes to dealing with economic interests of Canadians abroad, we get an entirely different attitude and response from the Prime Minister. It is a sort of quiet diplomacy that sees Canadian jobs and Canadian interests going down the drain. The problem in our fisheries is a perfect example. We have similar problems in the auto industry, with a loss of jobs, and similar problems in the electronics industry with the export of jobs to the United States. There is nothing done until a crisis is reached.
We have an announcement that there is a kind of war that will exist, or a no-man's land area, in the fisheries on both our coasts. A good part of the responsibility has to be directly attributed to the federal government's negotiating approach.
For over a year now there have been violations of the agreement on both coasts, and we have seen no public response coming from the federal government to redress the grievances of Canadian fishermen. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment and, no doubt, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) will say, "Well, Canada lived up to its side of an interim agreement." The problem is that interim agreements with the United States, another federal system which operates somewhat differently from ours, in which the executive branch of the government is not able to enforce automatically an agreement in a way that can be done on this

side of the border, are precisely the kind of agreements into which the Government of Canada should not enter.
We should not enter into an interim agreement if that means we enforce our side of it in advance of the United States side, in a way which is detrimental to the interests of Canadian workers, whether they are fishermen or any other group of Canadian workers. Surely that is what we have here. 1 hope that this is a warning to the government for future courses of action, that any agreement entered into between Canada and the United States in the fisheries should not be enforced one day earlier on the Canadian side of the border than it is enforced on the American side of the border.
The second point I would make concerns the negotiating position of the Canadian government on this matter. For the last few months it has not been something of which Canadians should be totally proud. They have taken one position in substance on the east coast, and they have taken another position on logic on the west coast, and a third, as I understand it, in terms of the Alaska region. We cannot have a whole series of conflicting arguments and get anywhere in serious bargaining with another nation.
In conclusion, 1 want to say that I hope that the government, with the United States, can reach an early agreement in this area and that the agreement will be one which will be enforceable simultaneously on the part of both countries which will then simultaneously bring benefits to those employed in the fisheries on both sides of the border.

My point of order is not with respect to that as much as it is to a statement which was made by Mr. Speaker in the midst of verbalizing his thought processes with respect to whether the motion was in order. It was not a ruling, because Mr. Speaker in fact allowed the motion to be put.
However, in the course of his remarks Mr. Speaker did say that there was some question as to whether there was jurisdiction for a member of parliament to raise such a matter. There was a question as to whether the jurisdiction lay within parliament or whether it was a matter between the government and the opposition. There was some question about whether there is a limitation of the rights of hon. members under Standing Order 43.
Point of Order-Mr. W. Baker
In the course of the question period which followed 1 looked into the matter to find out how far one may go and what one may cover in a motion under Standing Order 43. The relevant Standing Order reads as follows:
A motion may, in case of urgent and pressing necessity previously explained by the mover, be made by unanimous consent of the House without notice having been given under Standing Order 42.
I think the words of that order are quite plain. There is no question of jurisdiction, no question as to whether it is a matter between the opposition and the government in that regard. The question, the condition of the motion, and the condition which allows such a motion to be put, are purely and simply "in case of urgent and pressing necessity".
I have a caveat with regard to the verbalizing of the thought processes of Mr. Speaker leading to his decision to allow the motion to be put, because I think it is important that that right not be limited to any member. If there were any doubt about the question that we are dealing with, that is, the question as to whether or not there is a matter of urgent and pressing necessity involved, it is a fact that for the first time in living memory, I believe-perhaps I am wrong-the members of the staff of the House of Commons are picketing outside the building today.
I know nothing about the merits of the case or the rights of the case as yet, but I think I should say that it is important to the members of the House of Commons, to our relationship with the staff of the House of Commons, to our understanding of the situation, that the first step to be taken be the tabling of the documents. The House has decided that that is not so, but 1 hope that at some stage the House might consider changing its mind.
I rise to put that caveat with respect to the right of a member of parliament to use the provisions of Standing Order 43, its only limitation being that the matter be of urgent and pressing necessity, not the question of the jurisdiction under which the matter falls, whether it is the government's jurisdiction, the jurisdiction of Mr. Speaker, or of anyone else connected with the operation of government. Mr. Speaker found, by allowing me to put the motion, that that was the case today. But I want to make it very clear that it is important to the rights of all members of the House of Commons that there be no limitation on that jurisdiction. That was the purpose for which I rose. I wanted to make it very clear to the Chair and to my colleagues on all sides of the House.

I think the same applies to the question raised by the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Abbott). There are practices that should be changed, and I am glad he put the question to me.
I want to make it clear that on this occasion Mr. Speaker did not say that I had no right to raise the matter, nor did the minister by his intervention indicate that he felt thatwhat I had to say was trivial-in fact, just the opposite. But I wanted to protect the rights of members with respect to what I thought were, to put it mildly, a disturbing thought process by Mr. Speaker in dealing with this matter.

subsubtopic: MUNICIPAL DEVELOPMENT AND LOAN BOARD
speechtext: The questions that have been asked are not relevant to the operations of the Municipal Development and Loan Board. The board was established under the authority of the Municipal Development and Loan Act in August, 1963 to administer a $400 million loan program in accordance with the act, for purposes of promoting increased employment in Canada by providing financial assistance by way of loans to municipalities to enable municipalities to augment or accelerate municipal capital works programs. The salaries and expense incurred by the board and its staff were paid out of moneys appropriated annually by parliament. In June, 1969 the board had fulfilled all the responsibilities assigned to it under the act and accordingly terminated its activities as of that date. The board's last annual report was submitted as of March 31, 1969. Since 1969 the Department of Finance has been collecting interest and repayments of principal on the loans outstanding. The Crown's sole financial interest consists of the loans outstanding. As of December 31, 1977 the loans outstanding totaled $194,891,549.16.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I must say that it has been rather interesting to observe the cross-fire which has been going on in the House, in the media, and in other areas. I know that the expressions on both sides of this issue are made with great feeling, because there is strong feeling, and the issue crosses all political lines. At the same time there has been some games playing, some jockeying for position and what not, but it seems that the minister's only defence in trying to explain this particular proposal is that if members oppose this bill they are deemed to be in bed with the separatists. Of course that is absolutely wrong. If the minister were correct it would certainly be well to observe that there are a lot of people in this country who are sympathetic to the separatist cause. That off the cuff defence must be dispelled, and it really is a weak defence as far as the minister is concerned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Not only weak, it is contemptible.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
In spite of the all-out effort which has been made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and his colleagues on the government side to drum up support for this

legislation, and in spite of his attempts to explain it, along with the kind of drama that has unfolded, as well as the war of words which is being waged between the Minister of Finance and his counterpart in Quebec, one cannot help but observe that the positions are indeed solidified, and in fact there is a major confrontation developing. Throughout, the federal government continues in its mission to attempt to divide and conquer. In the process, I submit to you, sir, that it is not attracting any new wave of support.
One might sympathize with the Minister of Finance. I think it would be fair to say that he is simply a front man in this particular battle for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde). I repeat, the stand that the government has taken on this particular issue is not gaining any support. As a matter of fact the Globe and Mail of May 18, 1978, said as follows:
The federal government has made itself look like a dictatorial central government and it hasn't a defender in sight.
That pretty well summarizes the position of the support this piece of legislation has across the country.
The April 10 budget and this particular bill provide a classic demonstration of how this government has floundered over the past ten years. During that ten years it has battered the economy and has created a state of political instability. The budget and this legislation, in my view, should have served as a major catalyst toward creating a climate of stability and confidence. Instead, they have created a climate of confusion and uncertainty and have placed further strains upon Confederation.
I believe that the provinces quite correctly consider this to be another major intrusion into the provincial domain, without adequate consultation. I am sure all members of the House recall the western premiers' task force on constitutional trends. As a result of that meeting in Brandon in 1977 a report was published. At that time the western premiers documented some 50 examples of federal intrusion into the provincial domain. This year in Yorkton, during a similar conference held in April, the premiers again noted with regret nine further examples of federal government intrusion into the provincial domain. The governments that are representative of these provinces are not all of one political stripe. One needs only remind hon. members that there are two Progressive Conservative governments, one Social Credit government, and one New Democratic government involved.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: There is a great dearth of Liberals.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The Liberals are not there, and they will not be there for a long time as far as western Canada is concerned. There will be no question about that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: A lost species.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
and purposes it was an extension of that new found spirit of cooperative federalism which was supposed to have emanated from the federal-provincial conference in Ottawa in February. However, this is what the western premiers had to say about that new found spirit of cooperation after the Minister of Finance brought down his budget in April. Again, in the communique which the western premiers submitted after their April 13 meeting, they said this:
The federal budget had directly contradicted the spirit of federal-provincial co-operation and consultation which the February conference had been intended to foster and could be prejudicial to ongoing discussions on national unity.
We all remember those very pious words and that profound proclamation about this new spirit and new generation of cooperative federalism. We can now only conclude that those statements were empty, hollow gestures. All they were doing at that time was tuning the machine for an expected spring election. After the budget, the Minister of Finance changed the rules of this scheme after it was introduced, but only for one province. Alberta was excluded originally and was not allowed to benefit from the rule change. The Manitoba government, as has been pointed out by other speakers, wished to use its share of the program used for purposes which it felt was best for the provincial economy, just as Quebec had done with its selective sales tax cuts. In the process, Manitoba was turned down.
The western premiers had further comments to make about this. I quote again from their communique arising out of the April 13 western provincial premiers' conference:
The premiers stressed that they were not debating the principle of the sales tax cut as a fiscal measure, but they were sharply critical of the unilateral and intrusive way in which it had been put forward.
That hardly resembles a spirit of cooperation in consultation. It is more like confrontation. It is more like arrogance and an insensitivity toward the powers of the provincial governments. They took very grave exception, and rightly so. The fact that the provinces did not participate in the decision concerning the federal compensation formula which has the effect of treating Canadian taxpayers differently, depending on the region in which they live, is certainly an issue that we find bothersome and irritating. This gets to the very heart of this whole fiasco.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) highlighted the problem when he said that in Bill C-56 the government has divided Canada into three distinct regions: Alberta is treated as an outcast with no benefits; Quebec is given unique and special treatment; and the other eight provinces are given varying degrees of benefit. We have a precedent whereby we deal with one province differently than with the others. We have a situation in which Alberta is not included as a legitimate participant in this whole proposal.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), who is supposed to be representing the interests of Albertans in cabinet, gave what I believe to be a somewhat incredible speech in which he seemed to scold Albertans for their prosperity. It reminded me of a modified version of a
Income Tax Act
former minister of agriculture from that province, Senator Bud Olson. He continually attempted to defend the government of the day, trying to sell it to the people of Alberta, rather than selling the problems of the people of Alberta to the government. After listening to the hon. minister's speech I have to say that he was much more effective in opposition than he was when attempting to defend this proposal. After listening to, or reading his speech, I think one will find that the defence seems to knock holes in the argument that Albertans need to have someone in cabinet.
The minister spoke of the discrepancy between the rich and the poor provinces and of how Albertans should be ashamed of themselves in requesting a better deal. He attempted to justify the government's treatment of Alberta in the provisions of the budget and of this bill. I should like to quote a passage from his speech at page 5696 of Hansard for May 24, where he said:
There is a logical reason why the Minister of Finance in his attempt to bring and hold our country together should address himself to the problem that exists in Canada, a huge tax rate in some provinces and a lower tax rate in other provinces. Similarly, in some provinces there is a high sales tax rate, and in another province there is no sales tax rate at all. The Minister of Finance, in my opinion, was quite right in addressing himself to that problem.
No one is denying the concept of and the need for equalization between the provinces; quite the opposite is true. It is something that is supported by this party, and indeed it was created under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). The concept of equalization was valid then and it is valid today. There is certainly no argument about that fact. The problem which the minister states, is already being addressed under the concept and formula of equalization. We already have a very large equalization scheme which cost the provinces of Alberta, British Columbia, and Ontario something in the order of $2.5 billion in 1977-78, and will cost something in the order of $2.7 billion in this fiscal year. It is a costly program, there is no question about that, but it is worth while. It is the price we pay to maintain some semblance of balance in Confederation from a financial and economic point of view.
Another point which seems to have been overlooked in this debate-I am surprised that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce failed to make reference to it-is that it should be noted and not be forgotten that since 1973 Albertans had not been receiving world prices for gas and oil. Because of this, something in excess of $10.4 billion in revenue has been forfeited by the people of Alberta toward equalizing the price of oil and gas across the country. In effect, this amounts to a direct subsidy to the rest of the country at the expense of Alberta. Further, it should be recognized that the maintenance of the artificially low prices has had and will have some effect upon investment and upon the advancement of our technology in the area of further development of our energy resources.
Let us not forget as well the days when there was a major confrontation between the former minister of finance, the hon. Don Macdonald, and the government of the province of Alberta. During that period the climate did not augur well for the development of energy resources. As a matter of fact the

actions of that minister and of the Prime Minister against the province of Alberta bordered on a hate campaign. I can remember him describing the minister of energy of the province of Alberta as "dripping with venom", and other vindictive descriptions of that nature.
I do not believe there is any other major, important, natural resource that is extracted and sold in this country that does not command a world price. This must be looked upon as a benefit to Canada given by the people of Alberta. I should say one more thing, Mr. Speaker, and that is that you do not hear Albertans complaining about this situation and reminding Canadians of it every day. It is a matter that I bring up today only to balance some of the misstatements and half truths that have been expounded in this House by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
The minister spoke of the tremendous benefits the Syncrude project has brought to the people of Alberta, and there is no question about that. It should not be overlooked, however, the benefit that has accrued and that will accrue is not confined to the people of Alberta but is affecting all Canadians in terms of security of supply and in terms of attainment of self sufficiency in energy.
It should not be overlooked, either, that over $200 million worth of contracts for equipment and machinery was let to enterprises in the province of Ontario, nor that in excess of 500 contracts were awarded to 176 Canadian contractors worth close to $400 million, that is, contractors not only in Alberta but in British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec. The spin-off effect to the people of Canada has been enormous.
Let it not be forgotten that it was not only Albertans who were employed on this massive project; literally people from every corner of Canada worked on it and shared in the benefits. Of course that is as it should be, and no one is arguing about it. If further projects of this magnitude are undertaken I am sure the same conditions will apply.
Recently I had occasion to visit one of the CanMar drilling ships working in the Beaufort Sea on one of the Dome Petroleum projects. It was very interesting to me that almost the total marine crew came from Nova Scotia. Other people who were working on the rigs were from other parts of the country. When you have a resource that is being developed in one part of the country, one province, the benefit of that resource accrues not only to that province but to the whole of Canada.
The federal government has not been favourable to Alberta. It has been favourable and it has done what is necessary only when it was absolutely required for it to do so in terms of the national interest.
I am glad the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is here because I want to make reference to a project that has irritated the provincial government of Alberta. That is the Petrosar project. Just last week the premier of the province of Alberta again made a comment about that project. He pointed out that this project takes some 16 per cent of the
[Mr. Mazankowski.l
Canadian oil supply from Alberta and ships it to Sarnia below the world price, and with it a number of Alberta jobs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Did he mention all the other jobs being created by Syncrude?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Yes, that has been mentioned. Yes, the Ontario government and the federal government did participate in that venture. I also point out that before the ink was dry, some $200 million worth of contracts were let into Ontario for the supply of equipment and materials. It has been quid pro quo. There is no question about that.
Alberta is interested in broadening its economic base. It is vital that it establish a manufacturing base, given the fact that the resources which are the subject of the wealth of Alberta today are depleting resources. Certainly the economy has to be diversified. The premier of the province of Alberta said that the Petrosar project set the Alberta petrochemical industry back some five to ten years. He described it as one of the worst decisions ever made in Canada. As a national project, the premier indicated that Petrosar is a disaster.
As I said earlier, there is a genuine desire, and I must admit there is a need, for Alberta to diversify, to broaden its economic base, to do further processing of its natural resources and products of agriculture. The Petrosar project certainly stymied Alberta's efforts toward further expanding the petrochemical industry.
This House should be reminded of the fact that today, in terms of manufacturing activity, Alberta only accounts for some 5.3 per cent of the manufacturing activity in Canada. Ontario accounts for some 51 per cent, and Quebec 26 per cent. Between the two central Canadian provinces, they command some 77 per cent of the manufacturing activity of this country. It is difficult to overcome that reality. Nevertheless, every effort should be made to ensure that we can diversify and that we can establish an effective and efficient economic manufacturing base in the province of Alberta.
This is why members of the Conservative party feel so strongly about the Hall report. In the Hall report we have, in addition to a transportation charter, an economic blueprint which, if followed, should assist western Canada in furthering its manufacturing and processing activities, particularly as they relate to agricultural products. We believe it is important that we build upon our natural strengths.
I wish to quote from the May 15 edition of Maclean's in which Andy Snaddon, chief editor of the Edmonton Journal, commented on this very subject. I quote from page 12:
What Albertans really want is to develop their province so that when the oil and gas is gone they'll still have a strong economy. That means just input into tariff hearings, it means a national system where each province has better representation at the decision making level ...
As for Albertans, we kind of like being able to sit in on the game and play with the other fellows, now we've got some chips of our own. We don't have to hope the nice players from Ottawa and Toronto will give us a piece of their winnings if we're good boys. We kind of like it. And it makes for a better game.
June 2, 1978

What he is saying is that, in spite of it all, we have done reasonably well. No thanks to the efforts of the federal government, we have progressed and will continue to progress.
Another area that I as a westerner should not overlook is the high level of tariffs which the federal government has established over the years to protect central Canadian industry. It has been estimated, and this again has emanated from the western premiers' conference, that it costs western Canadian consumers an estimated $1 billion a year. This represents something in the order of $500 for every household in the western provinces in any given single year.
I simply put these things on record at this time so that this whole question might be put into perspective and all this might he taken into consideration. I suggest that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did a disservice to Canada in failing to tell the whole story about Alberta's real role in Confederation and its commitment to the unity and economic viability of this nation.
I also wish to comment on an assessment provided by the head of the C. D. Howe Institute, Carl Beigie, who in Calgary last month had this to say, and I quote from a CP story in the May 5 Globe and Mail:
Alberta will be the only so-called 'have' province in Canada within two months.
Mr. Beigie told a conference on economic and social trends in western Canada that under current government definitions, Ontario will move in the have-not range with the pending natural gas price increase. Unless the federal government changes its definitions, Alberta will be paying a large part of the Confederation bill.
Mr. Beigie went on to say:
Alberta cannot be a long purse to finance federalism. The people are getting tired of it and I don't blame them.
I am not sure whether that comment reflects accurately the opinions of the people of Alberta. Nevertheless, the obligations and commitments of Alberta to the rest of the nation are very clear. We do not often hear the kind of complaint Mr. Beigie has raised, but if Alberta is to be excluded from federal programs and from tax benefits such as the one we are debating today, I suggest their generosity and patience will run out.
The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce have only one crutch upon which to rely in justifying Alberta's exclusion from the purchase tax measure. It is the new tax incentives for heavy oil and tar sands development, and I should like to deal with that aspect for a few moments.
First of all, there can be no question but that the development of new energy resources is for the benefit of Canadians as a whole. As for the government's concern for heavy oil, 1 must point out that ministers opposite discovered heavy oil only a couple of years ago. It is surprising, really, that we should still have a heavy oil industry in this country after all the discouragement it has received. It has only survived thanks to the efforts of various companies which have tenaciously held on through difficult times.
Income Tax Act
Throughout the debate, speakers on the government side have referred to this bonus which Alberta will receive. 1 think we ought to look at it from the point of view of the effect on the whole country if this source of energy is not developed. Based on National Energy Board demand predictions, Canada's oil imports will by 1985 be costing anywhere from $6.8 billion to $8 billion a year depending on the world price of oil. Payment on this scale will have a direct impact on our already precarious balance of payments position and further weaken the economy.
Jack Gallagher, president of Dome Petroleum, has outlined the effect which large foreign oil imports will have on the Canadian economy, in a speech made to the Canadian Institute of Strategic Studies last October. He stated:
The economic impact of importing one million barrels per day of foreign oil at $15 per barrel has a negative effect on the economy of $5.5 billion per year. In contrast, using one million barrels per day of domestically produced oil at the same cost delivered in Toronto creates a positive annual economic benefit of $15.6 billion which includes payments to the various levels of government of $6.2 billion ... In addition to the economic benefit of $15.6 billion from domestic oil... (Canada would realize) a saving in foreign exchange of $5.2 billion per year."
Those are astounding figures. The calculations are based upon 1977 dollars, and $15 is used to represent the price of a barrel of oil up to and including 1985. If that price is adjusted to $20 the impact would, of course, be considerably magnified.
Against this background, the need to develop our non-conventional oil reserves readily becomes apparent. Yet the government has, I suggest, been dragging its feet in promoting the development of heavy oil upgrading plants. We all remember that five years ago there was an oil crisis affecting this country. It was a signal the government should have heeded. At the present time our first synthetic oil plant is coming on stream. Unfortunately, we have not made very much progress in the development of our resources in the heavy oil field or in furthering another Syncrude project.
It is true that a lot of bold and exotic promises have been made. The federal-provincial conference ended with a whole series of announcements concerning energy projects which were being considered. But that is about all. The provisions in the budget are a help, there is no question about that, but we must establish the priorities clearly. Do we want the oil to be produced, or are we mainly interested in obtaining a high level of return from royalties and taxation, in which case we shall get neither?
I have received a letter from the president of the Husky Oil Company which is interested in the establishment of a heavy oil upgrading plant in the locality of Lloydminster, Saskatchewan. He recognizes the initiative which has been taken by the government, but adds that unless the actual numbers which the taxation people come up with are somewhat unexpected, the provisions in the budget will not make that particular plant a viable entity. So the trade-off we were supposed to have been given in this budget as citizens of Alberta is, transparently, not too advantageous. I contend we ought to embark on an aggressive program to develop our heavy oil resources. Governments

must reduce their take if they really want production to expand. Royalties and taxes must be reduced.
According to a recent study undertaken by the Canada West Foundation, taxes and payments to all levels of government now represent approximately 70 per cent of the pre-tax profits of the mineral resource industries. This compares with 53 per cent only five years ago. Backing off on taxes and royalties imposed on the development of non-conventional oil reserves in no way represents a give-away to the industry. The "corporate welfare bums" charge certainly does not apply in this case.
Consider, for example, the proposal by a consortium of 21 companies, including Petro-Canada, to build a heavy oil upgrading plant in eastern Alberta. It has been pointed out that this $600 million plant cannot become viable under the existing royalty and tax structure. Before the proposal can move from the negotiating table to the drawing board, royalties payable to Alberta will have to be reduced by some $500 million, and federal taxes by the amount of $400 million. We have to ask ourselves: would the remission of taxation to this extent really represent a loss of revenue? The answer is, no. If the appropriate fiscal regime is not provided, the upgrader will not be built, the heavy oil will stay in the ground, and the government concerned would get no revenue at all. If, however, the plant is constructed under a revised royalty and tax structure, royalty and tax benefits alone will, over a 20-year period, yield $2,675 billion to the Alberta government and $2.05 billion to the federal government. Moreover, these figures do not even begin to take account of the spin-off benefits which such large energy projects would naturally produce, more particularly in terms of the impact upon the balance of payments and the security of oil supplies.
I might mention a project which is proposed by the Husky Oil Company for an upgrader in the Lloydminster area. This has been an "off again, on again" type of project. Quite frankly, the government of the province of Saskatchewan and the Government of Canada have failed to provide the leadership necessary to get this project off the negotiating table and on to the drawing board.
Summing up, I reiterate my concern about the way in which the government has divided the country by this ill-considered measure. I protest strongly the terms Alberta is receiving under Bill C-56 and the rather shameful way in which government spokesmen have attempted to make Albertans feel they are something less than good Canadian citizens. As to the claim made by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce that the provisions in the budget relating to the heavy oil industry will make up for the unfair tax treatment given to Alberta under the sales tax program, 1 do not believe it can be sustained.
Be that as it may, I believe that in spite of this government, Alberta will continue to shoulder its load and to do well. I know that Albertans will continue to be good Canadian citizens. If Bill C-56 has served no other purpose, it has done one
[Mr. Mazankowski.l
useful thing. I believe it has laid to rest once and for all the myth that is being spread around Alberta that the province needs a representative in this cabinet. If the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) suggests that Bill C-56 is an example of how Alberta's interests are looked after, I can only conclude that this government has not learned very much since the period 1968 to 1972. During that period of time there were two ministers representing the province of Alberta and two government members of parliament. Subsequently all went down to defeat in the 1972 election simply because this government chose to ignore the concerns and wishes of Albertans.

In this connection, and quite in contrast to some of the quotations read into the record by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) who spoke just before me, I would like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post on April 12 of this year relating to the federal budget.
