The first major thrust in the budget is the one which has been much debated on the floor of this House and across the country, the attempt to strengthen consumer buying power, to get more goods and services moving, and to create
Income Tax Act
more jobs by cutting retail sales taxes. All economists agree that that is the most effective level at which to make a cut because it has a direct, immediate, and obvious impact upon the price of goods on retail shelves. Since those taxes are imposed essentially by the province, a unique federal-provincial taxation arrangement was obviously required to make the cuts possible. The net result of this taxation arrangement, if it can be successfully concluded, will be a very significant saving for Canadian consumers, more than $1 billion altogether over the next six to nine month period.
I would like to refer again to some local commentary about that particular measure. If hon. members are curious about what this proposal will mean to a large rural constituency like mine in western Canada, or to communities like Weyburn and Estevan in the southeastern corner of my constituency, I refer them to a newspaper published in my constituency, called the Weyburn Review. Not long ago, in the April 27 edition of that newspaper, the newspaper undertook to survey a group of businessmen in that particular community to get their reactions to the sales tax proposal. The headline on the story in "Sales Tax Reduction Encourages Major Buys," and the subheading is "General Reaction Positive".
The survey of the business community in the Weyburn area done by this newspaper revealed a generally positive reaction. The chamber of commerce in that community, as quoted in this story, pointed out that this one measure in the budget alone could have the impact of saving half a million dollars or more for the consumers in that one community. When we extrapolate those figures across a constituency like Assiniboia, and include other communities across the province of Saskatchewan and across Canada, the magnitude of the saving for consumers and the importance of this measure become obvious.
Apart from the question of the economic impact of that proposal to cut sales taxes, the measure is also significant for at least two other reasons. First, it demonstrates that federal-provincial conferences, like the one held earlier this year-they began last fall and carried on throughout the winter and into the early spring, but I refer particularly to the conference held in February and the others which led up to it-can in fact work to the positive advantage of Canadians.
Second, I think the measure demonstrates once again that it is important in this day and age for us to have in Ottawa the kind of determined national leadership required to cope effectively with the threat of separatism in this country.
After we have dealt with the sales tax measure, the second major thrust in the budget consists of a series of enriched tax incentives in three key areas to strengthen the private sector of our economy without government interference. The areas affected include, first of all, the field of energy development, which has been discussed in the House this afternoon. While these measures in the budget are not, admittedly, a complete answer to the energy development challenges that we have in this country, they will provide a significant encouragement,

June 2, 1978
Income Tax Act
particularly for the development of heavy oil reserves in western Canada.
The second area affected by the tax incentives is the transportation system, again with special emphasis on encouraging rail improvements on the prairies and through the mountains to the west coast to try to alleviate one of the problems that has occupied a lot of time and attention in the House in the last couple of weeks with respect to grain movement to export positions. The tax incentives provided in the budget to assist the railways should help us to resolve the difficult bottleneck which exists from time to time on the lines through the Rockies.
The third area is with respect to incentives for industrial research activities which could be important, for example, for such western manufacturing firms as those producing short line farm equipment.
I think it is obvious from the points I have mentioned that this budget does have special significance for western Canada because virtually every one of its major provisions has a positive impact on the prairies. But there are two other measures contained in the budget which even add to that case. First of all, there is the provision which will allow two million Canadians owning registered retirement savings plans to have more flexibility in the way in which they cash in those plans and use the proceeds. As everyone knows, the law requires that RRSPs be wound up before the age of 71 and that the proceeds must either be used to buy a life annuity or be taken into income as a taxable lump sum.
With the new budget there are now two more options that are available, the purchase of a fixed term annuity until the age of 90, or the use of a new investment vehicle which has been created by the budget called the registered retirement income fund. For retiring Canadians and those who are planning now for their eventual retirement by purchasing a registered retirement savings plan, those changes will be welcome indeed; they recognize the kinds of representations that have been made on this point by Canadians across the country, including many in the constituency of Assiniboia.
Finally, as a special western emphasis in this budget I would mention the provisions regarding capital gains taxes. The existing rollover provisions exempting family farms from the capital gains tax have been widened by this budget to allow the same tax advantages for incorporated family farms. That is a move which, I am sure, many westerners have been suggesting for quite some time, and I am pleased to see that the Minister of Finance has responded to the representations we have been making on that point. Obviously we must keep working with respect to the capital gains tax matter because more changes are yet required, but I think it is obvious that we are moving in the right direction.
It is instructive to take a look at the history of the development of the capital gains tax in this country. The capital gains tax theory or principle was first developed in the late 1960's and early 1970s in the ongoing process of tax review and tax reform. When the idea was first presented, particularly in the House of Commons, it seemed that once you had established
[Mr. Goodalc.J
the principle, there could not be many important exceptions to it. But over the course of time it has been demonstrated that substantial and important dents have been put in the idea that there cannot be any exceptions or changes to the fundamental theory or principle.
The first major deviation from the principle had to do with the family farm rollover which I mentioned a moment ago. It was a justifiable exception and one that has served reasonably well the farming community in this country, although I do not think it has yet been extended far enough. In the most recent budget, the extension of that special condition will apply to incorporated family farms as well as unincorporated family farms. Last year the tax law was changed in relation to capital gains taxes so that a farmer or a small businessman, for example, could dispose of a particular asset in order to reinvest in another capital asset of a similar nature. Previously that transaction was subject to the capital gains tax. Because of the change last year, that transaction is no longer subject to the capital gains tax in so far as the proceeds of the sale of the first capital asset are used to reinvest in acquiring replacement or similar property that the taxpayer intends to purchase. That is an important and useful change in the law and one that I most certainly support.
I think that additional changes in the field of the capital gains tax are most certainly needed, and I would like to suggest three ideas that I hope the government will seriously consider over the course of time because they are justifiable, particularly in their application to farmers and small businessmen in this country. First, I think of the valuation day problem which existed in 1970, 1971 and 1972. Everyone recognizes that in that period of time in western Canada capital values, for farmers and small businessmen especially, were artificially low because of the depressed economic conditions affecting agriculture, and in particular the grains industry. The problem with the capital gains tax now is that capital values have risen to more reasonable levels. Some would argue that the levels are excessively high, but they are considerably higher than they were in 1971-72. The fact of the matter is that that capital gain which is now taxable is artificially high because the valuation day value is artificially low, and this creates a particular burden upon farmers and small businessmen in my part of the country.
It could be alleviated to a certain extent by applying a formula of indexation to ease the burden of that low valuation day value. You could also take the other approach, if indexing is not technically possible to accomplish the job; you could apply an average over certain years, perhaps 1965, 1970 and 1975, and average the values together, taking those three years or a broader span of time, to get a more realistic base value upon which to base the capital gains tax law. But whether it is done by indexation, by the averaging formula or by some other method, we have to consider the problems created by that artificially low valuation day value across a great portion of western Canada.
Second, I should like the government to consider seriously the prospect of allowing farmers and small businessmen.
June 2, 1978

because of their peculiar economic position, their importance to the economy of this country, and because they do not have much choice about making major capital investments which they have to make if they are going to be in the business of farming or if they are going to operate their business enterprise, to be in a position of making a capital gain which is tax free by restricting it to a once in a lifetime opportunity so as to eliminate virtually all the speculators.
The principle of a once in a lifetime option is not something that is peculiar or unhead of in our taxation laws; it is a well recognized principle that goes back a considerable number of years. I think that the same principle that has been established in the past in our tax laws in other connections can well be applied to this case in relation to capital gains taxes, and it would help to alleviate the burden which falls at present on small businessmen and farmers.
Obviously some terms and conditions would have to be applied to the exemption. A logical condition to be applied to it is that the farmer or small businessman would have to be engaged in that enterprise for a certain number of years in order to qualify for the exemption, so that one could not simply become a farmer one day and claim a capital gain the next. There should be some condition applied to ensure that one is dealing with a bona fide farmer or a bona fide small businessman. You might consider the application of an over-all limit on the amount of the capital gain which would be exempted. For example, you might take an average-sized Saskatchewan farm as the basic limit that would be exempted from the tax, or whatever terms or conditions are required in order to make the provision fair. I think it is an option that is justifiable and I would like the government to take a serious look at the possibility of providing that once in a lifetime exemption from capital gains taxes to farmers and small businessmen in this country.
I have another proposal which is tied in with the issue of a once-in-a-lifetime exemption. It is a somewhat useful suggestion. It would be an innovative approach to the manner in which farmers and small businessmen are being treated in the acquisition of capital assets. The large capital investments farmers and small businessmen have to make in their farming and business enterprises should be treated as if those investments were contributions to registered retirement savings plans.
In many cases farmers and small businessmen do not have a choice about the capital they are required to pour into their enterprises. If one looked at the list of their capital assets, one would assume that they are enormously wealthy. That is not true or realistic at all. That amount of cash is tied up in a way that is of little use to them in a cash sense until they retire and sell their farms and small businesses. They look upon the potential income from the sale of their capital assets as a large portion of their retirement incomes. To a large extent those expectations are frustrated by the fact that they are required to pay capital gains tax on those assets.
Income Tax Act
If we were to treat the investments which they made during their lives in capital assets as if they were contributions to registered retirement savings plans, two important tax advantages would be provided. For the young farmer acquiring the land, he would benefit from a special kind of tax deduction on the principal and not just the interest of his land payments. When it came to the point in time for retirement, as a retiring farmer he would benefit from the same tax rules which apply to a person who is cashing in an RRSP. That would be a considerable advantage over the normal tax rules which apply to those circumstances at the present time.
I hope the government will give serious attention to my ideas: the question of a realistic valuation day value; the possibility of a once-in-a-lifetime exemption from capital gains tax for farmers and small businessmen; and the proposition of treating the investments of farmers and small businessmen in capital assets as if they were contributions to registered retirement savings plans.
Apart from those initiatives which I should like the government to consider for the future, the April 10 budget was very much a "good news" budget for the people of western Canada. The same is largely true for the rest of the country as well. Some people, particularly hon. members of the opposition, like to depict the Canadian economy always in the gloomiest and most negative of terms. Any objective analysis would indicate that Canada has shown a steady pattern of economic recovery from the worldwide inflationary shock of the early 1970s which brought on a global recession. That recession affected Canadians less largely than our neighbours in virtually all western industrialized democracies.
The economic boom of the 1960s and the early 1970s tempted all of us-workers, management and governments- to live beyond our means and demand more from the economy than it could sustain. By 1974-75 inflation had been pushed to critical levels, pricing us out of world markets and bringing on a surge of unemployment. Since the fall of 1975, strong remedial action has been under way. The anti-inflation program was launched at that time, and that action is working. Despite all the warts, bumps and imperfections, it has shown results.
Growth of government spending at all levels now is coming down, with the Government of Canada leading that trend. It would be encouraging if the provinces would do as well. Wage and other income increases are beginning to return to more realistic levels. The basic trend of our inflation is declining toward that 7 per cent target which was set for the end of this year.
A lower exchange rate for the Canadian dollar is helping to restore our competitive position in vital world markets. Nowhere is that more evident than in the grain and beef industries of western Canada. The trade deficit of $500 million which we suffered in 1975 has been turned around to a $3 billion surplus in 1977.
With respect to employment, we have had to cope with an unprecedented number of new people seeking jobs, including

June 2, 1978

the postwar baby boom, and with social and other desirable changes, a greater number of married women in the labour force. The actual job creation record of Canada is second to none in the world. Nearly 300,000 new jobs were available in this country in the past year. Our long-term average in job creation is in the range of 250,000 jobs per year.
There are sound, fundamental reasons for confidence and optimism as we tackle the economic challenges which still lie before us. Measures like those contained in the budget, and like those contained in the small business and research and development packages announced in the past week by government ministers, indicate that the government is meeting those challenges in a realistic and practical way. This will have a beneficial impact on all Canadians, and particularly in my constituency.
We have seen another rather amazing and unfortunate development in this debate on Bill C-56. We heard it reflected in some of the heckling by hon. members opposite at the beginning of my remarks this afternoon. Most of us who believe in federalism and one united Canada find it somewhat difficult to believe, but the evidence seems to be mounting that the Premier of Quebec and the Parti Quebecois separatists in that province have found a certain number of vocal allies in Ottawa who seem to be aiding their separatist cause.

The latest focus of attention obviously is the sales tax provision in the budget which proposes a billion dollar reduction in provincial retail sales taxes with federal assistance. The basic idea was to bolster consumer spending power and to stimulate economic activity across the country. Since those taxes are provincially imposed, a special federal-provincial taxation arrangement was required to make immediate cuts possible. In essence, Ottawa offered to reimburse the provinces for most of their lost revenues if they in turn instituted a general sales tax reduction of 2 per cent or 3 per cent across the board.
The principle of that cut being a general one across the board is extremely important. The negotiations to set up that type of arrangement went on for three weeks or more prior to the presentation of the budget in the House of Commons on April 10. All of the provinces with the exception of Quebec agreed to the plan. For its own reasons, the Quebec provincial government declined to agree or disagree in the negotiations prior to the budget speech in the House of Commons. Essentially it refused to state a position one way or the other. Then two days after the federal budget speech, the Parti Quebecois government came forward in full detail with its own complicated plan, obviously a plan which had been worked upon in secret and without comment for an extensive period of time. No mention was made of it during the negotiations with the federal minister or the other provincial ministers.

Essentially Quebec proposed to eliminate its sales tax entirely on a few selected products which would have largely a beneficial impact in the province of Quebec. Instead of participating in a national effort to encourage economic stimulation all across the country by a general sales tax reduction, the PQ wanted to draw the federal government into financing a scheme biased in favour of that one province. Obviously that scheme would interfere with the free flow of goods and services across the country. It would tend to fractue the Canadian market.
Quite rightly, the federal government said no to the Quebec proposal. While provinces may choose to impose different sales taxes on different goods, which is their right clearly and unequivocally within the constitution, the Government of Canada should not contribute directly to the financing of those differences.
That is the essential and important point in this debate. The general sales tax reduction would essentially be neutral in its impact as between provinces, and it would not of itself contribute to different rates of tax on different goods and services in different provinces. Surely, that principle of non-discrimination between provinces is fundamental to Canadian federalism and to the maintenance of one common national Canadian market which is the federal responsibility.
The startling thing in all of this is that the opposition political parties have sided consistently with the PQ argument on this issue. Over the past two or three weeks the Conservatives have argued essentially in support of the Quebec government's notion that federal funds should be used to help different provinces build a kind of discrimination into the marketing of goods and services across Canada depending upon the province in which you happen to live. If the Government of Canada ever allows such a thing to happen with federal funds, Mr. Speaker, you can imagine where that would leave a province like Saskatchewan, for example; we would suffer very badly and so would the over-all national economy.
The tactics of the Quebec separatists on this particular issue are easy to understand. They want to break up the country, and they make no secret about that. Obviously, from that standpoint, they are going to make federalism as awkward as possible and they are going to make confederation as difficult as possible. As I said before, that was graphically demonstrated as late as yesterday when the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) made two more proposals to the province of Quebec in an attempt to resolve the impasse, to try to find a way out so that the federal principles involved in this issue could be protected along with the provincial aspirations of Quebec. That adds up to approximately five proposals altogether which the federal government has put forward for consideration, and it is significant in this particular instance, as in the others, that it was the federal minister who had to take the initiative to call the provincial minister. The Parti Quebecois once again rejected the proposals put forward,

which clearly indicates their determination to make the federal system in this country difficult, awkward and hard to manage.
The Parti Quebecois' position, however, is fairly clearcut and easy to understand. What is less easy to understand is the pro-separatist stance that has been taken on this issue by the opposition parties in this House. That such a stand would be taken by a supposedly federal political party is simply beyond comprehension, except perhaps for the political mileage they might hope to gain from taking that kind of posture.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ALLOWANCES TO HOUSEWIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was present in the House on February 27, 1978 when my colleague from Bellechasse listed the reasons which had prompted him to introduce the motion which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of having parliament adopt a measure authorizing payment of an allowance to housewives who remain at home to take care of their family instead of joining the labour market, the purpose being to ensure a global income corresponding to the family's needs by providing an additional family income to that earned by the father.
Several members expressed their opinions on that occasion and generally they were in agreement, except for one hon. lady who expressed objections which I simply cannot endorse, particularly as those objections were voiced by a female member. However, I do not want to belabour those reactions we noted at the end of the debate on the motion. The important thing is to show the soundness of that motion and try to direct the legislation so that Canadian housewives will enjoy a decent
June 2, 1978

allocation allowing them to provide an additional family income to complement the earnings of the father and, as I suggested earlier, corresponding to the family's needs. In this uncertain age in which we live, the home and everything it represents remain the focal point in our society. In Canada, the wife and mother remains the centre of family life even though her contribution to the development of her country from farming society to an industrial and urban society has greatly changed her way of life.
Studies have been made to determine the number of working married women and the reasons why they work. We should ask ourselves about the circumstances which have brought our society to create a female manpower of nearly two million in Canada.
Following seminars on this issue which were called "Women at Work", it was suggested that this situation was the result of automation, urbanization, social acceptance and changes in social needs. The unanimous opinion of working women is that no mother leaves her children needlessly and they generally admit that they would rather be at home, but they add that they must have another income to maintain a proper home for their children. Economic reasons are the most often mentioned by women workers, especially those whose husbands are low wage earners, that is who earn less than $6,000 a year. It is easy to conclude that the reasons why married women seek outside work are economic in nature. The great majority of women who work do so to improve the standard of living of their family.
At this time when our political leaders are looking for answers to the problem of unemployment that they do not seen to be able to solve, it would be a good idea to encourage housewives by giving them a fair income, which would make more jobs available for those who have a lower family income. Legislation which would provide a salary for housewives would give evidence of an understanding attitude on the part of the authorities towards all the wives, and especially those of the farmers who must work long hours to take care of their children and do their part of the farming chores. Jacqueline Lemay sings: "Half the world is a woman." Could it be that our society discriminates even against the disadvantaged women, who account for half of our female population? We seem to think that rural women still work only for the glory of God and not to earn a good living.
In the February 22, 1978 issue of the newspaper La Terre de Chez-Nous, I read a letter written by Mrs. Blandine Saint-Cyr, assistant at the rural commission AFEAS, Nicolet section. I think it might be indicated for me to quote that letter which describes well the work of women in rural areas. It is really very hard to describe the situation of women in an agricultural milieu. To be the wife of a farm producer is to work constantly in co-operation with one's husband, without ever getting a salary because one is not entitled to it. In the past, women did much more work on the farm and out in the
Housewives' Allowance
fields. Today, because of mechanization, a rural wife takes a more active part in the decisions concerning the business and outside affairs. She is more interested in the farming techniques to better understand and participate in the fairly important investment decisions which farming involves. In many cases, the women are also the ones who take care of the accounting. For that, they have to get additional training, take courses and attend meetings dealing with farming. They also have to take care of the family and do the housework. Rural women are not indifferent to school problems; they have to see to it that their children get a good education to enable them at a later date to have skills or a profession. To do so, they have to attend meetings and learn about the new teaching methods.
In spite of her many obligations she is also a member of the school board or the recreational committee. She finds it necessary to join other women of the urban community and this is why she is a member of an association like AFEAS and others. Some years ago, the members of that association made a study on women working with their husbands. They realized that many of them were not aware of the provisions of their marriage contract. With that study women have been made more aware of their situation.
I believe that the farmer's wife really works in co-operation with her husband as she participates in the decisions of the business and its day to day operations and in certain cases she is even co-owner with her husband. This occupation is very close to nature and very pleasant but it does not allow you to take a few weeks' rest in the south. This was the conclusion of the letter from that lady.
I also had the occasion to read a release published some time ago in 1970 concerning the housewife and the labour force. The release said, and I quote:
We should consider housewives as members of the labour force and the value of the services they render in their home should be part of the gross national product.
Such action would improve the image of housewives and reduce the frustration of women in North America.
In a speech at the North Amercian conference on labour statistics, in Houston, Texas,... the Director of the Women's Bureau of the Department of Labour of Canada, Miss Sylvia Gelber said that women working at home should be considered as members of the labour force.
And I agree with this opinion. Further, she made a very timely remark that I wish to quote as I found it perfectly logical:
Miss Gelber humorously pointed out that if a man hires a cleaning woman her services are included in the gross national product. However, if later he marries that woman she will continue to perform the same work, but the gross national product will be reduced since her work has no monetary value.
And yet there is not much difference as far as work is concerned. Whether or not he is married to the cleaning woman, she does the same work at home. I wanted to add those few words about the motion because, considering what is happening in various countries, the discussions on the matter and the inquiries made for several years I feel it would be

June 2, 1978
Housewives' Allowance
normal that the wife or the mother be rewarded some way or another for her work. It would be quite normal in our modern world where we often hear about social security. Therefore well balanced wages should be paid to the mother and this is why I support the motion. I dare hope that the government will finally decide to do something to try and really improve the lot of the wife and mother.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ALLOWANCES TO HOUSEWIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to have an opportunity this afternoon to participate in this debate. The motion addresses itself to a very serious problem in our society which is growing in dimensions and which is demanding more and more attention. Unfortunately, the problem does not seem to be very high on the list of priorities of the government. I am talking about the problem of unattached females who are forced, because of inequities in our social welfare system, to live in poverty. We have the spouse's allowance, and there are currently about 75,000 Canadians who are availing themselves of this. However, that does not solve the problem of unattached female pensioners. The motion which has been introduced by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) gives us an opportunity to dwell on that problem for a few moments.
There are a number of reasons why I believe that the hon. member has addressed himself to this urgent problem. Let us look at the family in society. The family is the centre, the core and the keystone of our society, and it is under attack like never before. There are a number of factors which contribute to this situation. There is a trend toward urbanization. Most Canadian people live in cities, and our cities are growing. The majority of Canadians live in big cities. The problem of the single parent is a growing problem, and it is having an impact on family welfare. Then there is the problem, because of inflation and economic conditions, that spouses are being forced into the labour field. The result of all these things means that the family is under attack, and children are the ones who suffer most.
On the other hand, what about the traditional family situation where one spouse works and the female spouse stays at home and becomes the homemaker? What happens to her? What encouragement or incentive does society provide to carry on the traditional family situation? None. Indeed, we throw disincentives in the way by not permitting the homemaker to qualify under the Canada Pension Plan. If the homemaker could qualify under the Canada Pension Plan, that would solve many of our poverty problems among pensioners and, especially, unattached pensioners.
The statistics are frightening. According to Statistics Canada, over 50 per cent of unattached female pensioners in Canada are living below the poverty line because they have nothing to fall back on. They have no spouse's allowance and nothing to fall back on except old age assistance. If they are too young to qualify for that, they have to resort to provincial welfare. If we were to take the enlightened step of allowing the

homemaker to qualify under the Canada Pension Plan, we would be satisfying two very important social objectives. On the one hand, we would be protecting the family unit because the family cannot survive without at least one parent being home as a homemaker. It cannot survive as a healthy family unit. On the other hand, we would be addressing the problem of poverty among unattached female pensioners.
My own family situation comes to me as an example. If my wife were to leave the family unit, I would have nobody to take care of my six children. The family would lose the maternal influence of the mother in the home, and I would lose the services of a qualified housekeeper. I could solve the latter problem by going to the labour market and paying out a substantial weekly or monthly amount for a housekeeper. That would not solve the other problem regarding maternal influence, but for the purposes of the Canada Pension Plan why can Canada not recognize the role of the homemaker? I say "homemaker" out of deference to the fact that not all homemakers are females. In Canada there are 10,000 males who are homemakers.
Homemakers could qualify under the Canada Pension Plan in a very simple way. The deductions which are made from the family income-and my family income is my salary-could cover both spouses for the purposes of the Canada Pension Plan. This would ensure that when my wife reaches the pensionable age and the children have gone off to raise their own families, my wife would not be forced into the humiliation of having to fall back on the means test welfare system we have and old age assistance.
It would ensure a certain amount of dignity for the retiring female spouse. It would ensure a reasonably adequate income for both spouses, if we take into account both Canada Pension Plan benefits coupled with old age assistance. Hence, we would be able to eliminate the spouse's allowance, which does not really satisfy the situation now in that it unjustly ceases after the death of the older spouse, a situation to which I hope this parliament will address itself before too long.
It would also ensure a reasonably adequate income, and you would be able to eliminate in the process the spouses' allowance, as I have said, as well as the guaranteed income supplement. The guaranteed income supplement, as we know, is obtained after a means test by a person who does not enjoy the benefits of the Canada Pension Plan and can only fall back on old age assistance and, by way of subjecting himself or herself to a means test, obtain the guaranteed income supplement which will give him or her an additional $109 a month. We can eliminate that procedure by making the homemaker eligible for the Canada Pension Plan.
Ultimately we will have to take steps to protect the family, and I would say that this should be the first step in that direction. The growth in the rate of marriage breakdown in Canada, the growth in the rate of divorce and the growth in the rate of malnutrition among Canadians is frightening, a fact that was revealed in this affluent society of ours in a study
June 2, 1978

commissioned by this government on nutrition in Canada which is now gathering dust on the shelves of the bureaucracy. Malnutrition is a serious problem in this country, especially among our children, since we have a situation developing in this country of single parent families with inadequate income; of single parents having to remain home with the children, or perhaps even being forced out to work; or the situation which I have already identified where both spouses are forced into the labour market because of inflation and the economic condition of the country today. All these situations result in the innocent, the children, having to suffer.
So it follows that just as we introduced some time ago into this country a universal family allowance program, surely we should follow with the next logical step and introduce a program which would encourage one of the two spouses to remain at home to ensure that the family is properly looked after in terms of nutrition, in terms of health care, and in terms of the supervision and the responsibility that goes with raising children.
The situation today is such that we have the blot, the scandal, the disgrace on the face of Canadian society of women being forced to live in poverty because their life expectancy is considerably longer than that of their male spouse. The result is that when their male spouse dies, they have nothing else to fall back on except old age assistance. They do not have old age allowance because it dies with the older spouse. Surely we as a society, as the mover states in his motion, should recognize the importance of the family, and hence the importance of the homemaker to the family, and provide incentives whereby the homemaker would be able to remain with the family to provide for all these things that are necessary in raising a family today.
I would find it difficult to put a price on my wife. There is no way I can replace the maternal influence that she provides in our family. If I were to lose her, I would have to pay $10,000 to hire a housekeeper, and that housekeeper would be entitled to the Canada Pension Plan which I would have to pay and she would have to pay. Therein lies the anomaly of the whole situation. Surely it would follow logically that we as a society should recognize that the homemaker, usually the female spouse, is performing a very necessary function in society, one that can be measured in monetary terms, as I have indicated; and it would seem to me to be relatively simple to add a provision to the Canada Pension Plan whereby the principal income earner of the family would have deducted from his or her income the necessary amount to provide Canada Pension Plan benefits for the homemaking spouse. It is simple justice. It would address this scandalous problem of poverty in Canada with our older unattached people, most of whom are females.
What can we say for a society that does not take these necessary steps to protect the very keystone of society, the family? The greatest threat to the family unit today is the threat brought about by the economic conditions of world and domestic inflation which forces both spouses to go into the labour market, or the threat to the family brought about by
Housewives' Allowance
the demands of modern society, the urbanization of society, resulting in marriage breakdown, again causing the family unit to be under direct attack and causing considerable suffering among the children. This is a situation which will reflect on our future society.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) shows great compassion when she makes speeches outside the House. Recently she made a speech to the National Conference of Canadian Pensioners in Nova Scotia. She made another speech recently to the Second International Congress of the World Federation for Public Health Associations. In all of these various public speaking engagements she expresses great compassion, and I am sure she is a very compassionate woman. I as one member of the House would like to see the Minister of National Health and Welfare express these same sentiments in the House, and I would like to see her translate these sentiments into legislative form. She could not make a better beginning than to bring amendments to the Canada Pension Plan to make it possible for benefits to be paid to the homemakers in this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ALLOWANCES TO HOUSEWIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity of speaking in this debate on motion No. 25, a debate which I have been looking forward to joining for quite some time because I think this is an important aspect of our social considerations and one that tends to trouble me in certain aspects. Because of this it is important that, first of all, I review the wording of the motion as the initial background to my remarks. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of having parliament adopt a measure authorizing payment of an allowance to housewives who remain at home to take care of their family instead of joining the labour market, the purpose being to ensure a global income corresponding to the family's needs by providing an additional family income to that earned by the father.
I should like to congratulate the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert). I have to say honestly that of all the people in the House whom we like and admire, he is certainly one of my favourite colleagues.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ALLOWANCES TO HOUSEWIVES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ALLOWANCES TO HOUSEWIVES
speechtext:
I think we can say that for a lot of us he reflects the character of his party. He is a man of rather old fashioned values and of gentle sentiments, except perhaps, like his party, in certain areas of justice, such as capital punishment. He is a man who would put forward this type of motion rather naturally because certainly he is a family man, a man with a large family, as we all well know. I do not mean that sarcastically, I mean it in a very real sense in regard to this motion. I am sure he has a great sense of value embedded in this motion. There is no question about the need for assistance, or at least understanding and support, in this area.
As the previous speaker stated, in our modern society with all its benefits one of the casualties or the fallouts is the family with its pressures, particularly those on the children. We are

June 2, 1978
Housewives' Allowance
aware of new family problems these days which are costly to our society. There is a need for some adult to stay home and give support to the children a good part of the time. Traditionally that role has been fulfilled by the housewife, the female spouse.
In this day and age due to a change in participation rate in the employment situation, it is becoming increasingly questionable how many housewives wish to stay home. Also it is uncertain how many housewives expect to be reimbursed or compensated for staying at home and playing the role of homemaker. That role is very satisfying to many women. Generally it is agreed that marriage and families are partnerships, which is enough of a reward. Also it is agreed that financial arrangements can be worked out between family members.
We must consider what effect a measure such as this would have on the economy. An adjustment would be necessary if financial remuneration was paid to homemakers remaining in the home, especially on a full time basis. In strict but sincere mechanical and administrative terms, how would these duties be measured? What would be a fair remuneration and compensation for the economic value of homemakers?
Economic activity is only a part of human activity. Our social accounting procedures and rewards should have recognized this. An economic service has been defined as one which may be done by someone other than the person benefiting therefrom. One economist has estimated that the monetary value of the housewife to her family is equal to the sum of her income from work outside the home and the replacement cost of the services she provides in the house, less the value of her personal consumption. Obviously this is a rather complicated subject, especially when the necessary details are considered. Some economists are arguing that the allocation and efficiency of non-working time may be more important to economic welfare than working time. These economists are trying to deal more directly with the sources of utility or well-being by estimating the dollar value of non-market activities.
This is being done in various ways in different centres. As a proxy for the gross national product, one economist has applied the actual costs of domestics for a year to the number of families with two or more members. Some economists have carried out elaborate studies which included the mistaken assumption that full time female employees do no housework. The time budgets of some 30,000 persons on 99 items in 12 countries were studied in 1972. These showed that married women with paying jobs are overworked in comparison with employed men and housewives.
In Canada, Hawrylyshyn of Queen's University, Kingston, has been doing interesting work on evaluating household activities from an economist's perspective for Statistics Canada. From his review of international studies, he concludes in general that it is found that the value of household services is about one-third the size of the g.n.p. which, to say the least, is a very substantial amount. I believe that the current g.n.p. for Canada is approximately $200 billion a year. It may be ranked with agriculture, industry and services. He makes a
[Mr. Philbrook.l
good argument for including this substantial sector in a complete generalized input-output framework to assist us in understanding the whole system, of which the market is a part.
Walker and Gauger at Cornell University in the United States have studied the potential contribution to the g.n.p. of valuing household work through the market costs of functions, the work status of the wife, the number of children, and the age of the youngest child. Estimates of time use in specific household tasks were used for each category of the wife as noted above. The total annual values of the contribution of the wife were calculated with a value per family unit for their samples and an annual national estimate. Several years ago, Gauger calculated the value of the annual services of a wife whose only child is 12 to 17 years of age at $5,300; while for a wife with four children, the youngest under one year, the value was $8,400. Those facts are technical and complicated, but they are important background information.
I mention these studies to illustrate that recognition of housework in the calculation of national accounts can be done and should be considered. Society would then have better information on the quantity and the relative monetary value of unpaid work which indeed may constitute an important sector. People could make informed choices based on their economic, social and psychic costs and pay-offs. Canadians could learn not to take for granted the tasks performed by millions of unpaid persons who contribute so much to our collective well-being.
I remember a cartoon not so long ago in the New Yorker magazine. It showed a woman with curlers in her hair, sipping coffee and reading a magazine. The remains of breakfast were still on the table, the garbage was exposed, and the house was in utter chaos as the husband entered the door. The caption read: "Remember you were wondering what I do all day? Well, today I didn't". There is dirty as well as satisfying work being done by women in the home every day to make our lives pleasant and comfortable. We should not consign this work to women alone, and we should recognize what is being done when it is being done.
My own experience dictates that we are taking a much more enlightened view toward the home situation these days. Certainly husbands do not hesitate to pitch in more that they did in the past. I do not know which social problem the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) had in mind when he proposed payment of an allowance for housework. I agree with him that every help should be given, all recognition should be given, and security should be assured for persons who are not available to work outside the home because of family responsibilities.
Also I see the need for much greater variety in the organization of our work life. We have begun already successfully to utilize flexible time as an important part of our work arrangements. There are other areas which should be explored more thoroughly. We have not yet reached a stage where part time work has been rationalized as a good working practice which would combine high productivity and fair return to workers. It is difficult to reach a general public consensus on this. Obvi-
June 2, 1978

ously it is a challenge for our unions, businesses and governments.
Approximately one-quarter of the female labour force currently is employed part time, but many must give up the fringe benefits which the rest of the labour force enjoy simply because a system for part time work has not yet been agreed upon. Regularized part time employment could benefits parents and enable them to utilize their skills and contribute to the family income and activities. In this way they would no longer be part of the isolated, lonely group we are learning about who have few contacts during the day while at home with their children.
Here we are getting down to the nub of the problem in a very social sense, in a personal human sense. Many mental health experts are currently recommending part time work for young mothers to help them overcome the sense of deprivation of not using their education and prior training, and to cope with the lack of contact and stimulation which they experience when they become new mothers. Is it not said that western industrial society has made motherhood a lonely, isolated state? There are efforts that society can make to enhance community life and reduce that isolation and the problems that go along with it, such as the emotional upset, alcoholism, this litany of the social problems we are all familiar with and associate with the problems of mothers or homemakers.
I agree with the hon. member for Bellechasse that many families need more income than the father currently earns, although in many cases it is a question of whether they do need the income or they simply need to rearrange their concept of lifestyle to stay within that particular income. It is no secret that we have committed ourselves to exploring all avenues through our income security and taxation system to ensure that families, who despite their best efforts do not have enough income and experience hardship. We are concerned about the sole-support working mothers, two-fifths of whom have incomes which place them in hardship categories. This is another aspect of the problems posed by an increasingly affluent society, another aspect of the paradox of our present way of life.
It would be ironic for us, Mr. Speaker, to agree with a motion to send women back to that so-called "women's place" because we now have unemployment. This situation was not caused by women. We need women along with men to help solve the problem. We need women in our government as well as in all sectors of society in planning and decision making responsibilities. Women and men of all ages can contribute and benefit our society as responsible family members and workers as well as good citizens. The hon. member has stated that he believes in equal pay for equal work. It is very difficult to enforce that principle if one believes that women do not really belong in the work place.
Labours of love, devotion and care should be rewarded by society, but the question is how and by whom, by what method of transfer? These are important questions this House should
Housewives' Allowance
debate further. I thank you again, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to debate these important matters in this House with my hon. colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this subject. It strikes me that it is a subject which is a great deal more important than some of those that have been raised in many of the debates we have had in this House. It seems to me we spend too much of our time dealing with alleged barn burnings and very little time dealing with basic, substantial matters which affect the homes, families and lives of most Canadians. I commend the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) for introducing this motion.
It is a motion which, of course, has within it an attempt to increase the equity in our Canadian society, and it is very timely in that respect. I believe that most western industrial nations have been moving fairly rapidly over the last 15 or 20 years toward this goal of equity, toward making sure that all members of society occupy a reasonable, equitable position and, generally speaking, toward some kind of guaranteed annual wage. This is a step in that particular direction.
Unfortunately, most countries, ourselves included, ran into some problems in the mid-1970s, from about 1973, 1974 on, whereby most of the western economies were badly affected by a very massive shift in dollars to the OPEC areas, and as a result most of these economies are in very weak shape. Canada at this particular point has a deficit of $11 billion. There has been much talk about this, and about having too many social security measures transferring too many dollars from one pocket to another. I do not support that particular contention. I believe that these kinds of transfers are extremely important and that this debate is important in that respect.
I am surprised to hear the opposition parties, particularly the Tories, talk of the need to cut back in some of these areas; for example, to cut back family allowances. I am also surprised, in dealing with this motion, that no one has mentioned the fact that the cost of this proposal is fairly substantial. However, the motion is certainly worth dealing with and I personally have believed all along that we should be moving toward some sort of guaranteed income.

I cannot accept that as a statement. I would be very glad to discuss the matter in this House because I believe I can find some references in this respect.
In terms of this debate, I would like to focus on two separate areas in the very short time that is left. One of them has to do with the nature of the family, and this is a basic area that the hon. member raises in his motion. The other matter, concerns the employment of women and the need for employment. I think these are two relatively important areas.
As someone who spent 22 years in the education field as principal of high schools before coming to this House, I share the great concern about what is happening to the role of the family and the home in society. 1 think that for a long time schools were victims of society thinking they should take everything on. Family responsibilities tended to disappear into the schools. The schools tended to become bureaucratized to some extent and in many ways they simply were not able to carry out the functions society was loading on to them.
It seems to me there is a traditional role for the family in society but I think there have been some changes in thinking about housekeeping and the role of the mother which should be taken into account in the present day. One of the major changes is that more and more women are getting equal education with men. The level of education is rising and very often full time housekeeping duties are not adequate to meet the desires of a particular person. Due to new gadgets and more equipment, homekeeping is somewhat less onerous than formerly. Family size has decreased considerably since the introduction of the pill.
There is a whole series of reasons why women in the home are looking for some other kind of employment. I cannot accept the notion that the only reason women are working today is that they cannot afford not to work. I think a great many women are working because they enjoy the satisfaction of being independent and because they are able to become involved in activities in which they are interested and for which they are trained. I think it is wrong to assume that we
June 2, 1978

can return to the kind of family structure we were involved in in the past.
We have to keep some of the foregoing in mind when looking for ways to solve the problem of remuneration for women in the home.
There has been a general feeling that if the participation rate of women in the work force were not so high, we would have many more jobs available for the young people coming into the labour market and therefore we would not have so much unemployment. There may be some truth in that but it is a relatively small factor.
School population in this country has increased from 2.7 million in 1951 to 6.3 million in 1971, or by 230 per cent. This is the shocking figure that leads to the one million people unemployed. It is not the fact that we are not creating jobs at a fast enough rate. In fact, we are creating jobs faster than any other country in the industrialized world. The fact is that there is a tremendous number of young people now in the work force. If you compare, Mr. Speaker, the 230 per cent increase in the number of people going to school with the 30 per cent or 35 per cent increase in the participation rate, you will see that we have a factor which is very serious. School growth in that period was seven times the rate of growth of the population.
I think we ought to consider the possibility of work-sharing, particularly for many married women in the work force who would like to spend more time in their homes and the many women at home who would like to spend time in the work force. Putting the two together you get the interesting notion of work-sharing and perhaps, more specifically, pairing.
There is a good reason why government should be looking at this method of solving some of our employment problems. We should be trying to match the people who want to do both

those things. Some studies that have been done on pairing indicate that the productivity of a pair is far greater than that of one person doing the job. When I was a school principal I found that two people sharing a full teaching load did a great deal more marking. There was a great deal more work done and the quality was excellent.
I should like to speak about several other aspects of this problem but I see that time is running out. I think we should look carefully at the idea of some kind of guaranteed annual wage. An aspect that has a good deal to do with women in the home is the notion of a guaranteed annual role. There are people in our society, women at home and people doing voluntary work, who should be supported. The notion of a guaranteed annual role that would have attached to it a guaranteed annual wage is worth looking at.
